What are emotions?

blocks.html:
• Emotions are energy. They are normal — nothing is wrong with having them.
  • Humans are the only beings who can think and feel, and also understand what they think and feel.

  • There are no good or bad emotions. Every emotion has its place and value.

R1: Recognise

blocks.html: Identify and recognise your emotions and their triggers (what caused them).
blocks.text: Identify and recognise your emotions and their triggers (what caused them).

blocks.html:
• As children, we don’t know our emotions well. As we grow, we start to notice them.
  • Often we just ignore, suppress or bury them. That doesn’t help.
  • In yourself: notice your body language and body sensations.
  • In others: read their non-verbal cues and body language. Notice the difference between what is said and what is really meant or felt.
  • Different people feel different emotions about the same person or situation, because of their past, background and personality.

blocks.html:
• We often pretend nothing happened, or deny what we feel. We push it under the carpet and hope it disappears.
  • Instead, accept it and express it:
    • If you are angry, tell yourself: “I am feeling angry.”
    • If you are hurt, tell yourself: “I am feeling hurt.”
  • There are no good or bad emotions. Expressing them is better than carrying guilt, blame, shame or fear.
  • Respecting your emotions releases pent-up energy.
  • When you respect your own emotions, you can respect others’ emotions too.

The amygdala hijack

blocks.caption:
In about 6 seconds, panic takes over and
the thinking brain switches off. A pause can stop it.

blocks.html: When we overreact or freak out, the brain can trigger an amygdala hijack. It is an old, instinctive response: flight, fright, fight or freeze.
blocks.text:
When we overreact or freak out , the
brain can trigger an amygdala hijack . It is an old,
instinctive response: flight, fright, fight or
freeze .

blocks.html:
• It happens in about 6 seconds, but takes hours to recover from.
  • The rational, logical part of the brain shuts down. Decision-making suffers.
  • Stress hormones flood the body. The whole body acts like there is an emergency.
  • Long ago, this saved us from wild animals. Today, there is usually no such danger.
  • Repeated amygdala hijacks cause chronic stress, long-term anxiety, wear and tear of the body, and harm health.

Story 1: Night shifts at
the Taj hotel

blocks.html: At 19, Prof. Shiva had not finished his graduation. His friends had moved on; his family was upset. He told himself, “Get back in control of yourself.” He walked into the Taj Coromandel in Madras and got a job as a front office assistant — on night duty (9 p.m. to 6 a.m., often till 8 a.m.).

At 19 , Prof. Shiva had not finished his graduation.
His friends had moved on; his family was upset. He told himself, “Get back in control of yourself.” He walked into the Taj Coromandel in Madras and got a job as a front office assistant — on night duty (9 p.m. to 6 a.m., often till 8 a.m.).

blocks.html:
• Self-awareness and self-regulation: Others mocked him for working in a hotel while they studied chartered accountancy. He stayed proud of himself and balanced his emotions.
  • The power of a smile: A smile is a great leverage point. It disarms angry people. He learnt to smile and greet guests with respect: “Good morning, sir.”
  • Empathy: Tired guests often shouted at him after long journeys. He did not shout back. He put himself in their shoes — they just wanted to reach their rooms and sleep.
  • The result: Many guests who shouted at first gave him a big tip or a gift when they left.

How the armed forces
resolve differences

blocks.html:
1. The commander has a task. He calls his subordinate commanders.
  2. They do war gaming — like brainstorming in a company. Each subordinate shares their plan openly and freely.

  4. The commander takes responsibility for the chosen plan.
  5. Each subordinate must carry out the order as if it were their own plan — even if it is the opposite of what they suggested. “Myself becomes secondary; my team becomes primary.”
  6. The order must reach the last soldier on the ground.

2. Turning
customer doubt into customer delight

blocks.html:
Lecture example — Prof. Kartic’s “Knowledge Theme Park” Around 2010, after the 2008 recession, many people started leaving jobs. His team served a client of 8 years. The client worried that new freshers didn’t have enough knowledge.

For months, the team showed PowerPoint decks, metrics and test results. The client still wasn’t convinced.

Listening deeper, they found the real worry: the client’s quality team needed to prove the value to their own business stakeholders.

At a conference, Kartic saw games used to engage young employees. So they tried something risky: let the freshers themselves create something creative — not slides — about the insurance domain, and present it directly to the client. They called it the “Knowledge Theme Park”.

The client was delighted: “You have innovated amazingly.” They saw the freshers’ knowledge first-hand.

3. Two cultures, one thank-you
email

blocks.html:
Lecture example — the merger In the mid-2000s, Prof. Kartic’s fast-paced startup merged with an older, slower, more stable company. Neither was right or wrong — they were just different cultures.

Every meeting became a blame game. Middle managers were sandwiched between both sides. This went on for months.

Then he accepted that both sides were good people doing their best. He listed the progress made, however small, and the efforts of the other side. He sent a thank-you email to the other company’s VP and director and his own director — with zero expectation.

That email won hearts on both sides. It brought positivity back into the working relationship.

Scene in the film EI lesson
The panda dreams of becoming the Dragon Warrior with no skills — just fire in the belly. A burning ambition is the first skill, even when the path is unknown.
He cries that he’s useless. The Grand Master says he is clinging to the past or anxious about the future. Be present. “Yesterday is history, tomorrow is a mystery” — focus on today.
His teacher can’t train him — until he notices the panda is motivated by snacks, and uses that. Everyone has different motivators. Leaders must find each person’s trigger.

blocks.html: Prof. Sivakumar’s practices:

6. Advice for team players

blocks.html:
• Value every teammate’s strengths. Everyone has positives and negatives. “What you appreciate, appreciates.” (Example: tennis players Leander Paes and Mahesh Bhupathi were world number one as a pair — far higher than as single players.)
  • Before going to your manager: understand the problem, your role, and the team’s shared goals. Don’t go just to complain — go with a possible solution.
  • Talk to the teammate directly first. If someone is lagging behind, tell them yourself. Don’t let it grow and then complain to the boss — you’ll lose a teammate. Go together and report the status, not “this person is the problem”.
  • Be assertive. Assertiveness means being firm, speaking with conviction and following your values — not being rude or disrespectful.
  • EI is a lifelong practice — and remember, others are there to support you.

blocks.text: Emotional intelligence

blocks.html:
• Emotions are normal energy and messages; no good or bad emotions.
  • EI = recognising, understanding and managing your own and others’ emotions.
  • Benefits: self-awareness, empathy, communication, decisions, conflict resolution, freedom from emotional baggage, health, leadership, productivity, job satisfaction. EQ often trumps IQ.
  • Viktor Frankl: between stimulus and response there is a space — our power to choose our response.

The 6R framework

blocks.html:
R Key idea
Recognise Name the emotion and its trigger; check body sensations, energy, intensity (1–10).
Respect Accept and express: “I am feeling angry / hurt.” Respect yours → respect others’.
Rationalise Process through journaling, talking, meditation, nature. Ask: what thoughts trigger it? How true are they?
Release Let go of buried emotional baggage daily.
Response-able Choose your response. Amygdala hijack: flight–fright–fight–freeze in ~6 seconds; hours to recover. Pause, water, breathe, walk away.
Resilient Be kind to yourself; carry lessons, not baggage.
